09.01.title: Atomic bonding and stiffness
09.01.html:
Why is steel about 200 times stiffer than rubber and 3 times stiffer than aluminium? Young’s modulus is not a property you can change by heat treatment or cold work, unlike strength. It’s set by the bonds between atoms: how steeply the energy rises when you pull two atoms apart.

The pair potential

Two atoms attract at long range and repel strongly when their electron clouds overlap. A classic model is the Lennard-Jones potential:

V(r)=4ε[(rσ​)12−(rσ​)6].

It has a minimum of depth ε at r0​=21/6σ, the equilibrium spacing. The force between the atoms is F=−dV/dr, which is zero at r0​.

Stiffness is curvature

Expand V around r0​:

V(r)≈−ε+21​S(r−r0​)2,S=dr2d2V​​r0​​.

So for small stretches each bond is a linear spring of stiffness S: Hooke’s law, straight from the shape of the energy well. For Lennard-Jones, S=72ε/(21/3σ2)=57.1ε/σ2.

From bonds to Young’s modulus

In a simple cubic packing, each bond carries the load on an area of about r02​, and a strain ϵ stretches it by ϵr0​. Stress =Sϵr0​/r02​, so

E≈r0​S​.

Covalent and metallic bonds have S of about 20 to 200 N/m at r0​≈0.25 nm, giving E of 80 to 800 GPa: metals and ceramics. Weak van der Waals bonds, as in solid argon or between polymer chains, have S≈1 N/m and give E of a few GPa. Rubber is softer still because it doesn’t stretch bonds at all, it uncoils chains.

Two bonus results

  • The attraction is largest at 1.109r0​. That maximum force sets a theoretical strength of roughly E/10 to E/30. Real materials fail far below it, for reasons covered in 09.03 and 09.12.
  • The well is steeper on the inside than the outside. A vibrating (hot) pair spends its time further apart on average: thermal expansion.

Worked exampleArgon, from potential to modulus

ε=1.65×10−21 J (10.3 meV), σ=0.340 nm.

  1. r0​=21/6⋅0.340=0.3816 nm.
  2. Bond stiffness: the analytic formula gives 0.8157 N/m, and a central finite difference of V gives 0.8157 N/m. The slope of the force at r0​ is −S, as it should be.
  3. E≈S/r0​=2.14 GPa. Measured values for solid argon are about 1 to 3 GPa.
  4. Peak attraction 11.63 pN at 1.1087r0​ (strain 0.109). Stress estimate 80 MPa, which is E/26.8.
  5. Vibrating with 5 % of the well depth, the turning points are 0.9669 and 1.0431 r0​, so the midpoint moves out to 1.0050 r0​. At 20 %, 1.0220 r0​. That growth is thermal expansion.
  6. A metal-like bond with S=50 N/m at 0.25 nm gives E≈200 GPa, about right for steel.

Exercise 1A stiffer bond

A diamond C–C bond has a stiffness of about 470 N/m at r0​=0.154 nm. Estimate Young’s modulus with E≈S/r0​ and compare it with the measured 1050 to 1200 GPa.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. E≈470/0.154×10−9=3.05×1012 Pa, about 3000 GPa.
  2. That is about 2.7 times the measured value. The simple-cubic picture assumes every bond lines up with the load. In diamond’s tetrahedral network the bonds are tilted, so they also bend and rotate, and fewer bonds cross each square metre. The estimate gets the order of magnitude right, which is what it is for.

09.02.title: Crystal structures
09.02.html:
A Swiss watch spring, an aluminium bike frame and a copper wire are all crystals: their atoms sit on a regular three-dimensional grid. Which grid a metal chooses decides a lot. Copper and aluminium (face-centred cubic) are ductile even at low temperature, iron at room temperature (body-centred cubic) can turn brittle in the cold, and titanium and magnesium (hexagonal) are harder to form.

Unit cells

A crystal is a small unit cell repeated in all directions. For metals, model the atoms as hard spheres of radius R that touch their nearest neighbours. Three cubic cells, with lattice constant a:

lattice atoms per cell atoms touch along R coordination
simple cubic (SC) 1 edge a/2 6
body-centred cubic (BCC) 2 body diagonal 3​a/4 8
face-centred cubic (FCC) 4 face diagonal 2​a/4 12

Atoms on corners are shared by 8 cells, those on faces by 2. So FCC has 8⋅81​+6⋅21​=4 atoms per cell.

Packing factor

The atomic packing factor is the fraction of space filled by atoms:

APF=a3n⋅34​πR3​.

For FCC, 4⋅34​π(2​a/4)3/a3=π/18​=0.7405, the densest possible packing of equal spheres. Hexagonal close-packed (HCP) stacks the same close-packed layers in a different order and reaches the same 0.7405. BCC gives 0.680, SC only 0.524 (polonium is the only element that uses it).

Density from the lattice

ρ=NA​a3nA​,

with A the molar mass. X-ray diffraction measures a very precisely, so this links atomic structure to bulk density.

Worked exampleBuilding lattices in code

  1. The code generates lattice points, counts neighbours at the smallest distance, and computes the packing factor from the formula and by Monte Carlo (400,000 random points in the cell):
lattice coordination APF formula APF Monte Carlo
SC 6 0.5236 0.5235
BCC 8 0.6802 0.6803
FCC 12 0.7405 0.7403
  1. HCP with the ideal c/a=1.6330: coordination 12 and APF 0.7405, equal to π/18​.
  2. Densities: iron (BCC, a=0.28665 nm) 7.874 g/cm³; copper (FCC, 0.36149 nm) 8.935 g/cm³; aluminium (FCC, 0.40495 nm) 2.699 g/cm³. All match handbook values.

Exercise 1Nickel

Nickel is FCC with an atomic radius of 0.1246 nm and a molar mass of 58.69 g/mol. Find the lattice constant and the density.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. FCC atoms touch along the face diagonal: 4R=2​a, so a=4⋅0.1246/2​=0.3524 nm.
  2. ρ=4⋅58.69/(6.022×1023⋅(0.3524×10−7 cm)3)=8.91 g/cm³ (handbook value 8.90).

09.03.title: Defects and dislocations
09.03.html:
In the 1920s physicists calculated how strong a perfect metal crystal should be in shear. The answer was thousands of times stronger than any real metal. Either the theory was wrong, or real crystals had a defect that let them slip easily. In 1934 Taylor, Orowan and Polanyi independently proposed it: the dislocation. Seen directly in electron microscopes in the 1950s, dislocations explain why metals yield, why they work-harden, and why they can be bent instead of shattering.

The ideal shear strength

Slide one plane of atoms over another by x. The resisting stress must repeat every atomic spacing b. Frenkel modelled it as a sine:

τ(x)=τmax​sinb2πx​.

For small x this must reduce to Hooke’s law, τ=Gx/a with a the spacing between planes. Matching slopes gives

τmax​=2πaGb​≈2πG​.

For copper, G=48 GPa gives about 7.6 GPa. A pure copper single crystal actually starts slipping at around 0.5 MPa, some 15,000 times less.

Dislocations

Instead of a whole plane slipping at once, imagine an extra half-plane of atoms squeezed into the crystal: an edge dislocation. Under shear only the bonds near its core need to break and re-form, one row at a time, like moving a ruck along a carpet instead of dragging the whole carpet. The stress needed (the Peierls stress) is tiny for metals with wide, smeared-out dislocation cores. When it has crossed the crystal, the top has moved by one spacing b, the Burgers vector.

Most metallurgy is the art of making dislocations harder to move: grain boundaries, dissolved atoms, fine precipitates and tangles of other dislocations all get in their way (09.05).

A one-dimensional model

The Frenkel-Kontorova chain captures the idea. A row of atoms joined by springs k rests on a wavy substrate with wells one spacing apart. Push every atom with force F:

  • A perfect row slips only when F exceeds the substrate’s maximum restoring force.
  • Put one extra atom in (a kink, the 1D analogue of a dislocation). It glides at a far smaller push, because the atoms near it sit partway up the wells already.

Worked exampleIdeal strength and a gliding kink

  1. Copper: G/(2π)=7.64 GPa. Measured single-crystal yield is about 0.5 MPa, a ratio of 15,279.
  2. The chain: 60 sites, spring k=4, substrate amplitude V0​=0.2 (units where a=1). A perfect chain slips at F=V0​π=0.6283 per atom, verified: it holds at 95 % of that and slips at 105 %.
  3. With one extra atom, relaxed to a kink centred at site 29.5 (tightest spacing 0.715), bisection on F finds that the kink starts to glide at F=0.00766, 82 times less than rigid slip.
  4. Softer springs make a narrower kink that is harder to move: k=2 needs 0.06016 (10.4 times less than rigid slip) and k=1 needs 0.18940 (3.3 times less). Wide dislocation cores, as in FCC metals, are why those metals are so easy to deform.

Exercise 1Aluminium and iron

Estimate the ideal shear strength of aluminium (G=26 GPa) and iron (G=82 GPa). Annealed pure aluminium yields in tension at about 30 MPa, and soft iron at about 150 MPa. Taking the shear yield as half the tensile yield, how many times below ideal are they?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Aluminium: 26/2π=4.14 GPa. Shear yield about 15 MPa, so 4140/15=276 times below ideal.
  2. Iron: 82/2π=13.05 GPa. Shear yield about 75 MPa, so 174 times below.
  3. Both are polycrystals with some impurities, so they’re far stronger than a pure single crystal, but still two orders of magnitude below ideal. Only tiny defect-free whiskers and nanopillars come close to G/2π.
